prompt.context_jp: 国会議事堂前に黒塗りの車___次々と滑り込んできた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 国会議事堂前に黒塗りの車___次々と滑り込んできた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits the opening scene.

feedback.correct_en: が introduces the cars as brand-new information to set the scene — this is the very first sentence and the cars haven't been mentioned before.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat 'the black cars' as an already-established topic, which doesn't fit a scene-opening sentence where the cars are just appearing on stage.

contrast_examples.jp: 黒塗りの車は、政治家の象徴だ。
contrast_examples.en: Black cars are a symbol of politicians. (topic — generalization, different function)

prompt.context_jp: 神林の口元には、いつもの隙のない微笑___浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 神林の口元には、いつもの隙のない微笑___浮かんでいた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for the smile appearing on Kanbayashi's mouth.

feedback.correct_en: が marks 'a flawless smile' as the new visible detail the narrator is presenting about Kanbayashi's face. The topic (口元には) is already set, so the smile itself is new information.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make '微笑' the contrastive topic ('as for the smile...'), but the smile hasn't been introduced yet — it's what we're being shown for the first time.

contrast_examples.jp: その微笑は、作り物だった。
contrast_examples.en: That smile was fake. (smile already introduced → は)

prompt.context_jp:
「総理は、まだお辞めにならないつもりでしょうか」。
神林___答えない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 神林___答えない。
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama just asked Kanbayashi a question. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: は marks Kanbayashi as the established topic — he was just asked a question, so the focus shifts to 'as for Kanbayashi, (he) doesn't answer.' The contrast with the expected response is exactly what は signals here.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would push 'Kanbayashi' into focus as new information, but he's already the addressee of the previous line; making him the subject-focus reads as if we're identifying who didn't answer among several people.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰も答えないなか、神林が口を開いた。
contrast_examples.en: Among those who said nothing, Kanbayashi spoke up. (new info → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「大事な仕事___、全部あの息子さんがやっておりました」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「大事な仕事___、全部あの息子さんがやっておりました」。
prompt.prompt_en: The old man is contrasting the important work with other tasks. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: は marks 大事な仕事 as a contrastive topic — 'as for the important work (as opposed to minor tasks), the son was doing all of it.' The implied contrast with less important duties is exactly what は signals.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would identify '大事な仕事' as the new-information subject, but here it's the object of やる; more importantly, the discourse is contrasting types of work, which is は's job.

contrast_examples.jp: 急ぎの仕事が一件あります。
contrast_examples.en: There's one urgent task. (introducing → が)

prompt.context_jp: 啓太の手___止まる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 啓太の手___止まる。
prompt.prompt_en: Keita has just heard Miyama is a Diet member's secretary. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: が reports the sudden, observable event of his hand stopping — a fresh, in-the-moment occurrence triggered by Miyama's announcement. Narration of newly-occurring physical reactions almost always takes が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame '啓太の手' as a familiar topic being discussed, but the focus here is the action itself happening in real time, not a generalization about his hand.

contrast_examples.jp: 啓太の手は震えていた。
contrast_examples.en: Keita's hand was trembling. (ongoing state about an established topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 「僕___そんな立派な人間じゃありませんし、政治には全然興味ないんです」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「僕___そんな立派な人間じゃありませんし、政治には全然興味ないんです」。
prompt.prompt_en: Keita is rejecting Miyama's flattering description of him. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: は sets up 僕 as the topic and carries an implicit contrast — 'as for me (whatever you may think), I'm not that kind of person.' Self-description denials almost always use 僕は/私は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make '僕' new-information focus, as if singling out who isn't great — but Keita is just talking about himself, not identifying himself among a group.

contrast_examples.jp: 僕がやります。
contrast_examples.en: I'll do it (as opposed to anyone else). (exhaustive identification → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「でも、顔だけ___いいんですよ、これが。」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「でも、顔だけ___いいんですよ、これが。」
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama is describing Keita to Kanbayashi. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: は after 顔だけ creates a strong contrastive reading: 'his face alone is good (but everything else isn't).' The 〜だけは pattern is a classic limiting/contrastive use of は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just identify the face as the good thing, losing the cutting nuance that he's lacking in every other respect — which is precisely Miyama's point.

contrast_examples.jp: 顔だけがきれいでも意味がない。
contrast_examples.en: Even if just the face is pretty, it's meaningless. (neutral subject-focus → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「大事じゃない選挙___あるんですか」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「大事じゃない選挙___あるんですか」
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama's cold retort. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: With existence verbs like ある, が asks whether such a thing exists at all — 'is there even one election that isn't important?' This is the new-information/existential が pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presuppose 'unimportant elections' as a known category and ask about them, which weakens the rhetorical jab. Miyama is challenging the very existence of such a thing.

contrast_examples.jp: そんな本はありません。
contrast_examples.en: There's no such book. (negating an established topic → は)

prompt.context_jp:
「でも、期待しないでください。僕は親父みたいには――」
「お父様___関係ありません」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「お父様___関係ありません」。
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama sharply cuts off Keita's mention of his father. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: は sets up 'your father' as the topic Keita just raised, and dismisses it: 'as for your father — that's irrelevant.' The 〜は関係ありません pattern is a fixed way of pushing a topic aside.
feedback.incorrect_en: お父様が関係ありません would oddly identify the father as the specific person who is unrelated, as if among a list of candidates — but Miyama is dismissing the whole topic Keita brought up.

contrast_examples.jp: お父様が来てくださいました。
contrast_examples.en: Your father kindly came. (new info, identification → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「小難しい政策___、有権者に浸透すると思っているんですか」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「小難しい政策___、有権者に浸透すると思っているんですか」
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama dismisses the value of complex policy. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: が marks 'complex policy' as the subject of an embedded clause (政策が浸透する). In subordinate clauses like 〜と思っている, the subject typically takes が rather than は.
feedback.incorrect_en: は in an embedded thought-clause like this would awkwardly try to topicalize 政策 inside someone's belief — Japanese strongly prefers が for the subject of an embedded predicate.

contrast_examples.jp: 小難しい政策は要らない。
contrast_examples.en: Complex policies aren't needed. (main-clause topic → は)

prompt.context_jp: 父___長く心臓を患っていたことを、自分はどれほど真剣に受け止めていただろうか。
prompt.prompt_jp: 父___長く心臓を患っていたことを、自分はどれほど真剣に受け止めていただろうか。
prompt.prompt_en: Keita reflects on his father's heart condition. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: が marks 父 as the subject of the embedded clause 父が長く心臓を患っていた, nominalized by こと. Subjects inside こと-clauses almost always take が, not は.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would try to topicalize 父 across the whole sentence, but 自分は is already the main-clause topic; you can't have two competing topics, and the embedded subject must take が.

contrast_examples.jp: 父は心臓が悪い。
contrast_examples.en: (As for) father, his heart is bad. (main-clause topic → は)

prompt.context_jp:
「この国で四年間にどれだけの選挙があるか、知ってるか」
「……いえ」
「国政選挙、地方選挙、合わせて三千七百から三千八百だ」
啓太___思わず息を呑んだ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 啓太___思わず息を呑んだ。
prompt.prompt_en: After hearing the number, Keita reacts. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: Keita is the established protagonist of this scene — narration switching back to his reaction uses は to mark him as the ongoing topic. Established characters reacting to information typically take は.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce Keita as new information, as if singling out who gasped among several people — but he's been the focus of the whole conversation, so there's no need to reintroduce him.

contrast_examples.jp: 突然、啓太が立ち上がった。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly, Keita stood up. (sudden visible event → が)

prompt.context_jp:
拍手___なかった。
しかしその沈黙___、これまでとは違う重さがあった。
prompt.prompt_jp: しかしその沈黙___、これまでとは違う重さがあった。
prompt.prompt_en: After Keita's confession speech. Choose the particle for the second sentence.

feedback.correct_en: は marks 'that silence' as a contrastive topic against ordinary silences ('this silence, unlike others, had weight'). The しかし and これまでとは違う signal contrast, which is は's specialty.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would simply identify the silence as having weight, losing the crucial 'but this one was different from others' nuance the narration is going for.

contrast_examples.jp: 急に沈黙が訪れた。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly silence fell. (new event → が)

prompt.context_jp: 「彼には、人を惹きつける何か___あるんだ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「彼には、人を惹きつける何か___あるんだ」
prompt.prompt_en: An old member of parliament comments on Keita. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: With the existence verb ある, 何か takes が — 'there's *something* about him.' This is the classic existential が pattern: presenting that something exists.
feedback.incorrect_en: 何かは is unnatural here because 'something' is being introduced for the first time as a vague new entity, not picked out as a known topic.

contrast_examples.jp: その何かは、まだ言葉にならない。
contrast_examples.en: That something can't yet be put into words. (now established → は)

prompt.context_jp: 「手加減はいらん。若いもん___はまだまだ負けんぞ」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「若いもん___はまだまだ負けんぞ」。
prompt.prompt_en: The Prime Minister boasts before serving. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: 負ける takes に to mark the opponent — 'lose TO young people.' This is a standard 〜に負ける pattern; the に points to the party you're losing to.
feedback.incorrect_en: で would mean 'at/with young people' (instrument/location), and を doesn't fit because 負ける is intransitive and doesn't take a direct object.

contrast_examples.jp: 決勝で強豪に負けた。
contrast_examples.en: Lost to a strong team in the final. (で = location, に = opponent)

prompt.context_jp:
「神林君、君、テニスは嫌いなのか」。
「___。ご覧の通り、捻挫をしてしまいまして」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「___。ご覧の通り、捻挫をしてしまいまして」。
prompt.prompt_en: Kanbayashi apologizes politely to the Prime Minister for not playing. Choose the opener.

feedback.correct_en: 申し訳ありません is the formal register required when addressing the Prime Minister — Kanbayashi is a senior politician but still defers in this setting. It expresses genuine apology while preserving professional distance.
feedback.incorrect_en: ごめんなさい is too casual/childish for addressing the PM, and 悪いね is colloquial peer-talk that would be wildly inappropriate from a faction chairman to the Prime Minister.

contrast_examples.jp: 悪いね、今日は無理だ。
contrast_examples.en: Sorry, can't today. (casual peers)

contrast_examples.jp: ごめんね、遅れて。
contrast_examples.en: Sorry I'm late. (friends/family)

prompt.context_jp: 「後援会の皆さんのご心中、___」と神林が低く応えた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「後援会の皆さんのご心中、___」
prompt.prompt_en: Kanbayashi offers condolences at the wake. Choose the appropriate phrase.

choices.text: 気にしないでください

feedback.correct_en: ご心中をお察しいたします is a set condolence phrase — humble form 察する acknowledging another's feelings at a time of grief. It's the expected register for a politician visiting bereaved supporters.
feedback.incorrect_en: わかります sounds presumptuous (claiming to share their grief flatly), and 気にしないでください is wildly inappropriate at a wake — it minimizes the loss.

contrast_examples.jp: ご愁傷様です。
contrast_examples.en: My condolences. (standard funeral phrase)

prompt.context_jp: 「これからは全て、私の___に動いてもらいます」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「これからは全て、私の___に動いてもらいます」。
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama lays down the law to Keita. Choose the word.

feedback.correct_en: 〜の言うとおりに動く is the set phrase for 'move exactly as someone says' — とおり captures the 'in accordance with/in the manner of' nuance Miyama needs to convey total compliance.
feedback.incorrect_en: 言うことに動く isn't a natural collocation; you'd say 言うことを聞く ('obey'). 言う方に doesn't form a coherent expression here.

contrast_examples.jp: 親の言うことを聞きなさい。
contrast_examples.en: Listen to your parents. (different collocation)

prompt.context_jp: 「___ぎっくり腰だ、___ぎっくり腰だから」と本人は呻いたが、担架は無情に救急車へと運び込まれていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「___ぎっくり腰だ、___ぎっくり腰だから」
prompt.prompt_en: The PM insists his injury is minor. Choose the word.

feedback.correct_en: ただの means 'just a mere/only a' — the PM is desperately downplaying his condition as 'nothing more than a back sprain.' It's the perfect fit for someone refusing to acknowledge a serious problem.
feedback.incorrect_en: ひどい would mean 'a terrible back sprain,' which contradicts his goal of minimizing it. 大した usually appears with negation (大したことない) and doesn't fit here.

contrast_examples.jp: ただの風邪だよ、大丈夫。
contrast_examples.en: It's just a cold, I'm fine. (downplaying)

prompt.context_jp: 「あんなことで辞任する___ないでしょう」。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「あんなことで辞任する___ないでしょう」。
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama dismisses the idea that the PM would resign over this. Choose the expression.

feedback.correct_en: 〜わけがない is a strong denial pattern meaning 'there's no way (he) would do X.' Miyama is emphatically rejecting the possibility that the PM would resign over a minor injury.
feedback.incorrect_en: ことがない means 'have never done' (experience) and is wrong tense/sense. ものがない doesn't form a natural denial pattern here.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が嘘をつくわけがない。
contrast_examples.en: There's no way he would lie. (strong denial)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が嘘をついたことがない。
contrast_examples.en: He has never lied. (experience)

prompt.context_jp: 「短期決戦です。小難しい政策が、有権者に___と思っているんですか」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「小難しい政策が、有権者に___と思っているんですか」
prompt.prompt_en: Miyama mocks the idea that complex policy reaches voters. Choose the verb.

feedback.correct_en: 浸透する ('to permeate, seep through') is the standard collocation with ideas, policies, or messages spreading into and being absorbed by a target audience. 政策が有権者に浸透する is a fixed political-speech collocation.
feedback.incorrect_en: 感動する means 'be moved emotionally' and is something people do, not policies. 成功する ('succeed') doesn't take 〜に in this sense and doesn't describe ideas reaching people.

contrast_examples.jp: ブランドが消費者に浸透する。
contrast_examples.en: A brand permeates among consumers. (same collocation)

prompt.context_jp:
「いいか、選挙戦はマラソンと同じだ」
「ぶっ倒れるのはゴールの後だ。それまでは___走るんだ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「それまでは___走るんだ」
prompt.prompt_en: Hiraichi rallies Keita. Choose the expression.

feedback.correct_en: 全力で走る ('run with all one's strength') is a fixed collocation. The で marks the manner/means of running — pouring full effort into the action.
feedback.incorrect_en: 全部に doesn't form a coherent manner adverbial with 走る. 全然 is a degree adverb that requires negation in standard usage and doesn't mean 'fully.'

contrast_examples.jp: 全力を尽くす。
contrast_examples.en: Give it your all. (related collocation)

prompt.context_jp: 「そげな言葉、言わんと。あんたは人の期待に___タイプやけん、結局は一生懸命やってしまうとよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 「あんたは人の期待に___タイプやけん」
prompt.prompt_en: Keita's mother describes his personality. Choose the word.

feedback.correct_en: 〜に弱い means 'be weak to / unable to refuse' — his mother is saying he can't stand up to people's expectations and ends up giving in. 期待に弱い is the standard collocation for someone who can't say no.
feedback.incorrect_en: 期待に強い isn't natural — 強い with に typically describes resistance (寒さに強い 'resistant to cold'), which would mean he's immune to expectations, the opposite of her point. 厳しい doesn't fit personality-to-pressure descriptions.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼はお酒に弱い。
contrast_examples.en: He can't hold his liquor. (weak against)

prompt.context_jp: Setting: Kanbayashi, a senior politician, apologizes to the Prime Minister for being unable to play tennis with him due to a sprain.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most natural for Kanbayashi to say to the Prime Minister?

choices.text: 申し訳ありません。ご覧の通り、捻挫をしてしまいまして。
申し訳ありません。見てください、捻挫しちゃったんで。
すみませんでした。捻挫があるんで。

feedback.correct_en: Option A maintains consistent formal register throughout: 申し訳ありません + ご覧の通り (humble 'as you can see') + しまいまして (humble continuative). All three pieces match the deferential tone toward the PM.
feedback.incorrect_en: B mixes formal 申し訳ありません with casual 見てください / しちゃった, creating a jarring register clash. C uses past-tense apology for an ongoing situation and the blunt 〜があるんで is too casual.

contrast_examples.jp: ご覧の通り、満員でして。
contrast_examples.en: As you can see, it's packed. (same humble pattern)

prompt.context_jp: Setting: Miyama coldly retorts when someone calls this election 'an important one,' implying every election is important.
prompt.prompt_en: Which retort sounds most natural and cutting in Miyama's mouth?

choices.text: 大事じゃない選挙があるんですか
大事じゃない選挙はありますか
選挙で大事じゃないのがありますか

feedback.correct_en: Option A uses が with ある to challenge the very existence of unimportant elections — a sharp rhetorical jab. The んです adds a confrontational 'are you really saying...?' tone fitting Miyama's coldness.
feedback.incorrect_en: B with は softens it to a neutral inquiry, losing the bite. C is grammatically awkward and over-complicated; native speakers would simplify to A.

contrast_examples.jp: 嫌いな食べ物があるんですか？
contrast_examples.en: Is there food you actually dislike? (same challenging pattern)

prompt.context_jp: Setting: At the climax of his speech, Keita admits the truth about his father in front of the angry crowd.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version best fits the gravity of Keita's confession?

choices.text: 父が金を受け取ったのは、本当だろうと思います
父は金を受け取ったのは、本当だろうと思います
父の金の受け取りは、本当だろうと思います

feedback.correct_en: Option A uses が for the embedded subject in the 〜のは clause — the standard pattern for nominalized clauses. 父が…のは…本当だ presents the fact cleanly: 'that my father took money is true.'
feedback.incorrect_en: B doubles up topic markers (父は + 〜のは), which is ungrammatical. C is overly bureaucratic and stiff — Keita is making an emotional public confession, not writing a report.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が来たのは事実です。
contrast_examples.en: It is a fact that he came. (same が…のは pattern)

prompt.context_jp: 「お待たせ」と歩み寄った総理___、神林は深く腰を折った。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「お待たせ」と歩み寄った総理___、神林は深く腰を折った。
prompt.prompt_en: Kanbayashi bows to the approaching Prime Minister. Choose the particle.

feedback.correct_en: に marks the target of the bow — 'bowed deeply TO the Prime Minister.' Directional verbs like 腰を折る (bow), 頭を下げる, 挨拶する all take に for the recipient.
feedback.incorrect_en: で would mean 'at the Prime Minister' as a location, which is nonsense here. を doesn't fit because the PM is the recipient, not the object being bent.

contrast_examples.jp: 先生に頭を下げる。
contrast_examples.en: Bow to the teacher. (に = recipient)

prompt.context_jp: ラケットが空を切るほど大振りなサーブ___、総理の腰を捻った。
prompt.prompt_jp: ラケットが空を切るほど大振りなサーブ___、総理の腰を捻った。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for the sudden bad serve.

feedback.correct_en: が introduces the over-swung serve as the new agent causing the injury — a dramatic, in-the-moment event being narrated. The serve hasn't been a topic before; it's the new cause.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat the wild serve as an established topic, but the sentence is showing us a fresh, decisive event that immediately leads to the injury — exactly what が is for in narration.

contrast_examples.jp: そのサーブは伝説になった。
contrast_examples.en: That serve became legendary. (now established → は)

prompt.context_jp: Setting: Hiraichi, a veteran election planner, scolds Keita for not appreciating his position — telling him plenty of people would kill for a chance to run.
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most natural for Hiraichi's gruff, mentor-like tone?

choices.text: 選挙に出たくても出られない人間が山ほどいるんだぞ
選挙に出たくても出られない人間がたくさんいらっしゃいます
選挙に出たくない人間が山ほどいるんだぞ

feedback.correct_en: Option A combines the vivid colloquial 山ほどいる ('there are heaps') with the masculine んだぞ ending — perfect for Hiraichi's blunt, mentor-from-the-trenches register. The meaning 'can't run even if they want to' is the whole point.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's polite いらっしゃいます is wildly mismatched for Hiraichi scolding Keita. C flips the meaning — 'people who don't want to run' — which destroys the rhetorical point.

contrast_examples.jp: 悩んでる奴が山ほどいるんだぞ。
contrast_examples.en: There are tons of people struggling. (same gruff register)

prompt.context_jp: Setting: Keita acknowledges that some people will forgive his father's wrongdoing, arguing politics requires getting one's hands dirty.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing best fits a public political speech?

choices.text: きれい事で政治なんかできない
きれいなことで政治なんかできない
きれいごとで政治はできるのか

feedback.correct_en: きれい事 ('idealistic / sanitized talk') is the fixed noun used to dismiss naive idealism — exactly what's being argued: 'you can't run politics on pretty words.' The なんか adds dismissive force.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's きれいなこと means 'beautiful things' literally and isn't the idiomatic phrase. C turns a declarative argument into a question, losing the rhetorical thrust of the original speech.

contrast_examples.jp: きれい事だけじゃ世の中は回らない。
contrast_examples.en: The world doesn't run on idealism alone. (same idiomatic use)
